prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, which opened the 10^-18 regime of frequency metrology and made it possible to test fundamental physics and gravitational redshift in the laboratory

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading all eight ballots. The new physical idea is concrete and original: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trapping-light shift, so many atoms can be interrogated at once without perturbing the clock transition. Ye's group then pushed accuracy and stability to roughly 10^-18, resolved the gravitational redshift over millimetre scales and used many-body effects in the clock. The results have been reproduced and surpassed in many independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others), which is the robustness I look for. Seven of eight members ranked B002, two of them first, so it is the broadest shared ground on the shortlist. The credited pair is also unusually clean for a modern prize, which matters when the three-person limit forces hard choices elsewhere (Higgs, IceCube, circuit QED and squeezed light all strain it). The physics is about understanding atoms and time to extreme precision, and the clocks now serve as probes of fundamental constants, dark-matter couplings and relativity. It is a discovery that nobody expected to reach this level when the clock lineage began.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is lineage overlap: the 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch, frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) already cover much of the clock story, so a lattice-clock prize could look incremental or technical, and Ye already shares in the 2005 recognition. A second objection is that the SI second has not been redefined and that ion clocks and the thorium nuclear clock compete for the same narrative. A third is that this is a precision instrument rather than a surprise: Mehlig and Pearce both ask whether a clock is a discovery or a technology. I think the content is distinct (lattice interrogation, magic wavelength, many-atom systematics and redshift tests), but the committee must make that argument in the citation explicitly.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks lattice clocks only eighth, noting that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured Ye's comb work and the clock lineage, and that competing approaches such as ion clocks and the thorium nuclear clock bear on timing.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, and it is my own main uncertainty. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and 2012 rewarded control of single ions. Neither addressed the problem Katori solved, which is how to trap thousands of atoms in light without shifting the transition, and it is that step that gives the statistical gain behind the 10^-18 results. I would argue that the lattice clock is a new physical regime, not a refinement of a known one. The nuclear clock is still at an early stage and I do not think it argues for waiting. If Mehlig can show that the committee prefers a mathematically sharper universality result such as KPZ, I would want to hear whether it has comparable independent reproduction across many laboratories. The experimental confirmation of KPZ statistics is mostly from one liquid-crystal system, with other realisations less clean, and that weighs against it for me.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B002 first because lattice clocks changed what can be measured: 10^-18 uncertainties, relativistic redshift at millimetre scales and a route to redefining the second, reproduced by many laboratories.
responses.response: I agree, and I would add that the decisive evidence is the cross-comparison between laboratories, because a systematic error in one clock would not survive agreement among several independently built ones. I differ slightly on timing. Kroll treats the redefinition of the second as unnecessary for a prize, and I agree, but I would not lean on it in the citation either, since it is a decision by metrologists rather than a discovery. The citation should rest on the physics: magic-wavelength trapping, the accuracy reached and the tests of relativity and fundamental constants that follow.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as an overdue, unambiguous discovery, recognised on the theory side in 2013, and offers Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as a defensible founder-based trio.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of the Higgs discovery, and I defer to Danielsson on particle physics. My reservation is attribution, not merit. Olsson and Pearce both point out that spokespersons and project founders are not necessarily those who made the decisive measurement, and the supplied names do not map onto the 2012 analyses. A prize that credits the instrument builders but not the analysis is one I would find hard to defend publicly. By contrast the lattice-clock credit is a clean pair with a clearly identifiable proposal and a clearly identifiable demonstration. I would like Danielsson to explain what makes these three the right individuals, because that argument decides whether B053 can be a preferred configuration or only an alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a launch of a new platform for strong correlations, observed by many groups, while acknowledging that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and that the experimental credit needs review.
responses.response: I find the field exciting and the reproduction by many groups persuasive. My hesitation is the attribution that Olsson herself flags: the first author of the key 2018 papers, Yuan Cao, is not among the credited names, and the early twistronics theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto predates the continuum model. Eriksson also raises the omission of Cao and Dean. Until the committee can settle who made which experimental step, I think B038 is the less secure configuration, and the unsettled superconducting pairing means the citation would have to rest on the flat-band platform and on the observation alone. I would not stand in the way of a well argued case, but I regard it as a closer call than clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the platform through which the macroscopic quantum phenomena recognised in 2025 became a general toolbox, while noting the contestable Blais/Girvin theory slot and his own proximity to the community.
responses.response: I appreciate that Johansson flags his closeness to this field, and I weigh his view with that in mind. Circuit QED is real physics, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits was only last year, and I think a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon would be a hard sell to the wider community. Kroll raises the same timing point. The credit problem is also acute, since four credited names are cut to three. For the mechanical-oscillator case, which Johansson ranks third and I rank second, I find we are in agreement that the quantum-classical boundary question is the attractive part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that lattice clocks are distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and how the citation should state that distinction.

The precise priority of the magic-wavelength proposal: I have not independently checked how far parallel proposals by other groups overlapped, although Katori's demonstration of the first strontium lattice clock is clear.
Whether the credited pair should be widened or kept at two, since Lemonde, Derevianko and the Sr and Yb clock communities also contributed.
Whether a three-person prize could be completed with a second distinct achievement without weakening the clean B002 pair.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and Ursula Keller groups, but none of these ties is to Katori, Ye or their laboratories, so no specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B002. I do work in atomic, molecular and optical theory and would want colleagues to weigh my enthusiasm for B002, B052, B060 and B063 with that field loyalty in mind. I also have a scientific closeness to the cold-atom and Zoller-related community through attosecond and many-body theory, which is not a conflict with the preferred configuration.
